11276-civil-government-in-the-united-sta:
John Fiske's 1890 textbook, Civil Government in the United States, explains American institutions by their origins, not only their present shape. Fiske, asked by Houghton, Mifflin to write a small book useful in schools and suggestive to general readers. adopts a historical method: he shows how institutions acquired their form and keep adapting to new conditions. Epigraphs from Pindar and Longfellow's Ship of State frame the work.

The book dedicates itself to hundreds of young friends Fiske met in studies of American history. Its argument is that government is perpetually modified, never finished. Generations of students learned civics from Fiske's clear, patriotic prose, and the book remains a readable introduction to federal, state, and local government.
15110-lessons-of-the-war-being-comments-:
Spenser Wilkinson's 1900 book gathers weekly comments on the Boer War, written from its eve on October 11, 1899, through the relief of Ladysmith. He frames the war as a fight for supremacy in South Africa between the Boer states and the British Empire, and he warns that weak policy leads to bad strategy. Buller's problems get close attention.

Later chapters follow delay, defeat, and collapse of Boer power, with pleas for the right commander and a clear national purpose. Wilkinson writes as a strategist for newspaper readers, not a memoirist. The book stands as a sharp, contemporary record of how Britain argued about its war week by week.
18602-the-fourth-r:
George O. Smith wrote this science fiction novel, first published in 1959 and reprinted by Dell in 1979. Its hero, James Quincy Holden, is five years old at the start, yet already talks like a grown scholar. At his birthday party he sips ginger ale while adults drink cocktails, wins at bridge, and debates his father on chance, logic, and the laws of games.

The book follows a child prodigy whose mind outruns his years, with gifts such as Kipling tales, a planetarium, and a geiger counter kit hinting at his bent. Smith writes with humor and a taste for bright talk. The novel is a clever, old-style tale of a super-bright boy.
19913-omaha-dwellings-furniture-and-impl:
Alice Fletcher and Francis La Flesche documented Omaha life for the Bureau of Ethnology. This study of dwellings, furniture, and implements appeared in the Thirteenth Annual Report. The Omaha's primitive homes were chiefly earth lodges. Bark or mat lodges came second in their account. Skin lodges, or tipis, served for travel and hunting. No sacred rites attached to lodge-building among the Omaha and Ponka, they note.

La Flesche, himself Omaha, gave the work insider knowledge. Fletcher's measurements and plans set an ethnographic standard. Houses encode kinship, season, and ceremony in their forms. The report preserves building knowledge elders still held then. It remains a foundation source on Omaha material culture.
20456-notes-on-certain-maya-and-mexican-:
Notes on Certain Maya and Mexican Manuscripts is a scholarly paper from the Third Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology. It studies the picture writings left by the Maya and the peoples of Mexico. Scholars of the time were just learning to read these old books.

The writer had lately obtained Léon de Rosny's work on the written documents of ancient America. It held a photo-lithographic copy of two plates, or rather one plate in two parts. Comparing such copies was the only way to study codices kept in distant libraries. The paper shows early American archaeology at work.
2096-a-smaller-history-of-greece-from-th:
William Smith, the great Victorian compiler of classical reference works, writes a compact history of Greece from its earliest times to the Roman conquest. Geography, the heroic age, and national institutions open the book. Smith wrote smaller histories for schools, cutting his larger works down to classroom size.

Chapters then follow Sparta and Athens, the colonies, and the Persian Wars from the Ionic Revolt to Marathon, Thermopylae, Salamis, and Plataea. Smith keeps the narrative clear and schoolroom-ready, and the volume still serves as a sound first history. The Greek chapters move briskly from myth to history, so pupils meet heroes before they meet politics.
21725-the-coxswain-s-bride-also-jack-fro:
Three tales by R. M. Ballantyne sit together in this volume, and the first follows lifeboat coxswain Robert Massey. Sturdy Bob, his mates call him, and handsome Bob to the women of his village. He leads the Greyton lifeboat, and his bride-to-be, a fair-haired fisher girl, waits ashore. Their smooth courtship opens the story on a calm, bright evening.

Storm and wreck soon test the coxswain and his crew, as lifeboat tales must. The two shorter tales that follow, Jack Frost and Sons and A Double Rescue, keep to Ballantyne's home ground of sea, weather, and brave deeds. Together they show his range in short form: love, duty, and rescue on a hard coast.
22457-the-verbalist-a-manual-devoted-to-:
Alfred Ayres wrote The Verbalist, a manual on speaking and writing with propriety. Its subtitle promises brief discussions of rules for good usage. Ayres corrects errors of grammar, wording, and pronunciation throughout.

His authorities fill a shelf of nineteenth-century language books. Bain's and Quackenbos's composition grammars stand among his sources. Cobbett's and Goold Brown's English grammars also guide him. Graham's and Crabb's books of synonyms settle fine word choices. Bigelow's Handbook of Punctuation handles stops and marks. The Verbalist distills all that learning into short, firm rulings. It preserves an age when correct English felt like a moral duty to many.
24086-over-the-rocky-mountains-wandering:
R. M. Ballantyne wrote this short adventure book for young readers of modest means, one of a set of small volumes sold for a shilling or two. Its hero is Will Osten, called Wandering Will, who comes home from a long trip to find his father dead. A bequest made during the California gold rush gave Will's father land there.

Will gathers friends and sets out to look at the property, so the tale turns to the life of miners in the gold country. A young lady Will met on an earlier voyage also crosses his path, and he must raise his fare home to England in a hurry. The book gives young readers travel, gold-rush scenes, and a hero always on the move.
24594-letter-to-the-reverend-mr-cary-con:
George Bethune English wrote this letter to the Reverend Mr. Channing, printed at Boston for the author in 1813. English had read Channing's two eloquent sermons on infidelity with interest, and he understood that their appearance owed something to a book he himself had lately published.

With deference and respect, English takes up arguments in the sermons where the reasoning seems less unexceptionable than the language. His letter is a polite but pointed piece of early American religious debate. Readers interested in Unitarian history will find it a sharp, courteous example of pamphlet argument.
26319-a-text-book-of-the-history-of-arch:
A. D. F. Hamlin's Text-Book of the History of Architecture, here in a seventh edition revised in 1909, served college students in the series edited by John C. Van Dyke. Hamlin, professor at Columbia, packed the volume with 229 pictures and diagrams, plus bibliographies, a glossary, and an index of architects. A restored Parthenon fronts the book.

Mid-book pages compare Anglo-Norman churches with French Norman work, setting Waltham and Peterborough beside Cerisy-la-Foret. Hamlin notes that English builders meant to vault their naves but mostly kept wooden roofs, with Durham, Norwich, and Gloucester vaulted only later. The book surveys building from antiquity onward, in clear order for classroom use.
29194-g-r-r-r:
Roger Arcot wrote this fantasy story about Brother Ambrose, a monk who has borne a thousand injuries with humility and charity. Insults, however, are more than he can suffer. Each time Brother Lorenzo heads for his beloved geraniums, watering pot in hand and devotions whispered from saintly lips, Ambrose's hatred seethes. The very fact that Lorenzo lives seems a mockery of justice.

Arcot frames the tale with an aged manuscript, De Necromantiae, and a wish, not too repressed, to pledge one's soul to the Devil. Strange memories and frustrated souls fill this fantastic universe. Readers get a darkly comic monk's tale, where petty hatred curdles into a bargain with evil, told with a growl in its title.
29341-the-story-of-the-great-war-volume-:
Francis J. Reynolds edited this fifth volume of The Story of the Great War, a history of the European war from official sources, covering the Battle of Jutland among its subjects. It is the fifth of eight volumes, illustrated with drawings, maps, and photographs. A second-anniversary section prints statements from the British, French, and German ambassadors to the United States.

Parts cover Austrian propaganda, operations on the sea, the campaign on the eastern front, and the Balkans. Later parts treat the Austro-Italian campaign, the Russo-Turkish campaign, Mesopotamia and Persia, the western front, and the war in the air. Readers get a contemporary illustrated history of the war at sea and on land, written from official sources in the war's second year.
30025-rugs-oriental-and-occidental-antiq:
Rosa Belle Holt wrote Rugs, Oriental and Occidental, Antique and Modern, a handbook for ready reference, in a new and enlarged edition printed in Chicago in 1908. The copyright runs from 1901 to 1908, and the enlarged edition appeared on October 10, 1908. Thirty-three full-page pictures, twelve in full color, with other drawings and a map of the Orient, fill the book.

A front picture shows an antique Tabriz silk rug owned by Mrs. L. G. Burnham of Boston. Its panels mark mosque floor squares for kneeling worshippers, with Tree of Life forms and a rich border. Six chapters treat rug weaving in Egypt, Persia, and Turkey, then India, Afghanistan, and Beluchistan, with miscellaneous rugs and weaving in Europe and America. Holt notes that the first edition of 1901 stood almost alone in its field.
33280-civil-war-experiences-under-bayard:
Henry C. Meyer's memoir records his Civil War service under Bayard, Gregg, Kilpatrick, Custer, Raulston, and Newberry during 1862, 1863, and 1864. A captain of the 24th New York Cavalry and brevet-major of New York Volunteers, Meyer privately printed the book in 1911. Its chapters move from enlistment and first picket duty to Cedar Mountain, Brandy Station, and the second battle of Bull Run.

Meyer writes as a cavalry officer who saw the war from the saddle, noting deaths, raids, and acts of courage among his men. The memoir's strength is its close, dated detail, chapter by chapter. For readers of Civil War history, it is a valuable first-hand record of cavalry service in the eastern campaigns, told by a man who lived it.
33314-h-r:
Edwin Lefevre's novel H. R., published in 1915, centers on a man who made a woman famous, a scene captured in its frontispiece of a woman petrified at the sight of him. Lefevre, author of Sampson Rock of Wall Street, writes of New York life, fame, and the price of success, with a sharp eye for business and society. The book is dedicated to Robert Hobart Davis, a friend whose support Lefevre warmly notes.

The tale moves through studios, offices, and drawing rooms, where talent, luck, and will decide who rises. Its hero, known only by his initials in the title, embodies the self-made man of the age. For readers who enjoy novels of American ambition, the novel offers a brisk, knowing portrait of fame and its costs.
33334-the-only-woman-in-the-town-and-oth:
Sarah J. Prichard's Only Woman in the Town and Other Tales of the American Revolution, published in 1898, gathers stories of the war as seen by women and townsfolk. Prichard, author of a history of Waterbury, writes of a town where one woman stands alone, and of other episodes where ordinary people face invasion, loss, and loyalty. The book was issued by a Daughters of the American Revolution chapter.

The tales' charm lies in their local, human scale, where the Revolution is felt in kitchens and streets rather than on battlefields alone. Prichard writes with warmth for her subjects and care for fact. For readers of Revolutionary lore, it is a pleasing collection of short, true-flavored stories from Connecticut and beyond.
33470-the-forge-in-the-forest-being-the-:
Charles G. D. Roberts's Forge in the Forest, copyrighted in 1896, tells the narrative of Jean de Mer, Acadian ranger and Seigneur de Briart, and how he crossed the Black Abbé. Its frontispiece shows Marc seated on a block just inside a door, a quiet scene before adventure. Roberts, writing of a province whose honored sons he praises, sets his tale in a strange fellowship of forest and forge.

The novel blends history with romance, as Jean moves through Acadian lands, facing foes, friends, and the hard choices of a ranger's life. Its prose is rich and evocative, suited to readers who love Canadian historical fiction. For fans of Roberts, The Forge in the Forest offers a vivid, old-fashioned tale of courage in a wild land.
4230-tom-swift-and-his-motor-cycle-or-fu:
Victor Appleton opened the Tom Swift series with this boys' adventure. Young inventor Tom Swift gets his first motor-cycle and is drawn into a mystery. A reckless ride, a smash-up, and a talk overheard in the dark set him on a chase. Suspicious men in an automobile join the pursuit.

The chase runs through storms, a strange mansion, and a final capture. Tom rides to Albany and follows clues with his hired man Eradicate. He faces a vindictive tramp and a gang of thieves. The book is also a period piece, full of early motor-cycles, touring cars, and a young inventor hero.
667-the-gutenberg-webster-s-unabridged-d:
This section of Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary, published in 1913 by Merriam under Noah Porter, covers words beginning with R. Entries give spelling, pronunciation, part of speech, etymology, and numbered senses, from R, the dog's letter that hurreth in sound, through Ra, a roe, and Rab, a mason's rod, and onward. Notes trace Greek, Latin, and Phoenician roots.

R brings a rough music to the page: roaring beasts, road tools, and Latin roots crowd together. Readers meet rare trades beside common verbs, each with its own history. The slice rewards slow browsing, where one letter's words show how English borrowed, bent, and kept its sounds.
7192-charles-philip-yorke-fourth-earl-of:
Lady Biddulph of Ledbury wrote this memoir of her father from the letters and journals he left in her care by his will. He was Charles Philip Yorke, fourth Earl of Hardwicke and vice-admiral in the Royal Navy. She admits her diffidence as a first-time author, yet argues that his varied life and his part in the affairs of his time deserve a fuller record than silence would give.

The memoir follows a naval officer and peer through many posts, letting his own papers speak where they can. Portraits face the text, and the dedication to his grandchildren marks the book as a family trust as much as a public life. Readers meet a man of action seen through a daughter's loyal, careful eye.
8353-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-53-1-co:
Corinth's church was quarrelsome, and Paul's first surviving letter to it answers its troubles in order. Factions, lawsuits, loose morals, chaotic worship, and doubts about resurrection each get a reply, firm but pastoral. The letter's center holds two famous passages: the hymn to love, which outlasts prophecy and tongues, and the long proof that Christ's resurrection grounds the believers' own.

It also preserves the earliest written account of the Lord's Supper. In Challoner's Douay-Rheims wording, Paul's advice keeps its older Catholic dress. For churches and readers, 1 Corinthians remains the practical guide to unity: gifts differ, but love binds, and no gift excuses disorder or pride.
8354-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-54-2-co:
Paul's second letter to Corinth is his most personal writing, and the Douay-Rheims text gives it in Challoner's older English. Writing to a church that doubted him, Paul defends his apostleship. He speaks of beatings, shipwrecks, and a thorn in the flesh he could not remove, and claims that strength shows itself in weakness. The tone swings between tenderness and sharp rebuke.

A warm appeal to give for poor believers in Jerusalem runs through the middle, and the letter closes with a call to examine themselves and live at peace. Readers find Paul the man here, weary and proud and hopeful at once. It is the New Testament letter that most feels like a private letter, written in the heat of a quarrel.
a-smaller-history-of-greece-from-the-ear:
William Smith compresses Greek history for students, from the geography of the land and the heroic age to the Roman conquest. His contents move in clear order: the rise of Sparta and Athens, the Greek colonies, then the Persian Wars from the Ionic revolt through Marathon, Thermopylae, Salamis, and Plataea.

Chapters on Athens under Pericles and the three periods of the Peloponnesian War follow, then the Thirty Tyrants, the death of Socrates, Macedon's rise, and the age after Alexander. Smith, a famous classical editor, writes plainly and keeps dates and causes in view. Generations of school readers learned their Greece from this compact, orderly survey.
capek-r-u-r:
Capek wrote R.U.R. in Czech, and Czech readers meet the play here in its first tongue. Artificial workers pour from Rossum's factory to serve mankind. Made only for labor, they gain grievances, leaders, and at last the will to rebel.

The drama, first staged in 1920, coined the word robot for all the world. Beneath the marvel runs a hard question about work and worth. Capek gives even his rebels a claim on pity. In its own language, the play shows its wit and rhythm best, a landmark of Czech letters and of modern drama.
charles-philip-yorke-fourth-earl-of-hard:
Lady Biddulph's memoir of her father, Charles Philip Yorke, Fourth Earl of Hardwicke, Vice-Admiral, draws on the letters and journals he left to her care. Biddulph, his daughter, writes with diffidence, since this is her first experience of such work, but her reasons seem to her unanswerable.

Her father's active, varied life, and the large part he played in his day's affairs, deserve a fuller account than reference works supply. Biddulph presents in outline a capable, energetic Englishman, loyal and devoted to sovereign and country. Readers of naval and Victorian biography will find the memoir a labour of love, rich in letters and journals.

govdocs-archive_org-nsia-GiesbrechtRicha:
Five writers joined in an investigative article about Richard Giesbrecht, an insurance salesman from Winnipeg. In February 1964, Giesbrecht gave the FBI evidence of a multi-man plot to kill President Kennedy. Later, he said, agent Merle Nelson told him to forget what he had brought them.

A witness with evidence of a plot, told to forget it, is the heart of many assassination controversies. The article examines Giesbrecht's treatment at the Bureau's hands and the evidence he carried. It preserves a Canadian side door into the case, reported by a team of five journalists.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-NaimanJasonR_Na: Harold Weisberg, in all likelihood, wrote this letter, dated January 15, 1970, to Jason R. Neiman. Weisberg's letters of that season usually pushed his books, his lawsuits, or his requests for documents. The file keeps the date and the addressee's name only. It does not summarize the letter's business, so no honest account can say which of those subjects this particular letter took up.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PlotkinStevenR_: nsia-PlotkinStevenR Plotkin Steven R: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, complete. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WroneDavidR_Wro:
David R. Wrone, a historian at the University of Wisconsin, spent years listing nearly everything written about the Kennedy assassination. His annotated bibliography holds 2,376 entries on the killing of John Fitzgerald Kennedy, and each entry carries a note from the author.

A bibliography with notes does more than list titles. Wrone tells the reader what each item is, who wrote it, and why it matters, across books, magazine articles, pamphlets, and official reports. For anyone entering the huge literature on the assassination, his volume works as a map drawn by a scholar who read the territory himself and marked the sound ground.
govdocs-archive_org-spiritual-authority-:
René Guénon published Spiritual Authority and Temporal Power in 1929, a short book with a firm claim. It states the Traditionalist doctrine of the two powers: priesthood above kingship, spiritual authority above temporal rule.

Guénon argues that healthy societies keep that order, with kings guarding a law they do not invent and priests guarding the truth that law serves. When rulers claim the highest place for themselves, he says, decline and confusion follow in every part of life. The book is central to his work. Readers meeting Guénon for the first time often start here, because his whole system appears in it in compact form.
lessons-of-the-war-being-comments-from-w:
Spenser Wilkinson published his weekly war comments as Lessons of the War in 1900. Archibald Constable issued the book in London and Philadelphia. Chapters begin with the eve of the South African war.

Titles trace a week's campaign, playing with fire, and Buller's problem. Wilkinson asks how weak policy leads to bad strategy. He presses for reinforcements and calls the war the nation's business. His comments ran while the Boer War still unfolded. Readers get a military critic thinking in public, week by week. A chapter asks simply for the right man to lead. Wilkinson later became a noted military historian at Oxford.
nasa-tm-19660001934-a-system-for-automat:
Neal E Reid at Goddard described a system that gathers radiation test data on its own, in this August 1965 report. Semiconductor devices, the parts of modern circuits, change under radiation. Testing them means logging many readings over long exposures. Reid's system uses a digital clock, a scanner, and a relay box to collect those readings automatically.

Automatic logging removes hours of hand recording. It also cuts the errors that creep into hand-copied tables. Radiation data decided which electronic parts could fly. A system that gathered the data steadily, day and night, made those judgments faster and firmer for the engineers who relied on them.
nasa-tm-19660015402-on-the-production-of:
P B Abraham, K A Brunstein, and T L Cline at Goddard asked where low-energy cosmic ray electrons come from, in this February 1966 paper. Cosmic ray electrons arrive from space at many energies. The low-energy ones are the hardest to trace, because the solar wind bends their paths and changes their energies on the way in. Their origins could lie in the Sun, or far beyond it.

Sorting those origins shapes models of how particles fill the solar system. The paper belongs to Goddard's energetic particles preprint series. Such electrons also affect the radiation setting near Earth. A clear account of their production helps both pure science and the practical work of shielding crews and instruments.
nasa-tm-19670019840-description-and-desi:
Loren W. Acker, Nick J. Sekas, and Seymour Lieblein, of NASA's Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, describe a test facility in this memorandum. The facility serves liquid-metal radiators and condensers, hardware that dumps waste heat from space power systems. Liquid metals carry heat well, but they must be tested on the ground first.

The contents show the facility's layout in detail. Separate loops handle heating, vapor, and cooling duties. Component sections cover piping, material selection, stress calculations, and pressure losses. A primary heater gets its own treatment. The document is a design record for engineers building or using such rigs.
nasa-tm-19710018260-the-effects-of-charg:
Walter A. Wappaus conducted this test series on spacecraft mirror coatings that control temperature by reflecting sunlight. The coatings were silvered and aluminized FEP Teflon films used as second surface mirrors. In orbit such coatings face electrons, protons, and ultraviolet light, all of which can darken them and spoil their cooling power.

Wappaus irradiated both coatings with electrons and protons at two energy levels and with ultraviolet light as strong as five suns. He also tested ultraviolet and charged particles together, as real space delivers them. The results show both coatings suffer more from higher-energy protons than from electrons of the same energy. Combined exposure hurt more than particles alone at high doses, while ultraviolet alone in vacuum left the coatings virtually unchanged.
nasa-tm-19710022892-skylab-three-axis-mo:
Michael T. Borelli of the Marshall Space Flight Center and Jack Templeton of Sperry Rand Corporation reported these results in June 1971. Their report was issued as NASA TM X-64609. Their subject was STAMP, the Skylab three-axis motion platform. The platform tilts and turns a load in three axes to mimic spacecraft motion for tests and training.

The report describes the system, states its performance requirements, and then walks through the test program section by section. Tests covered frequency response, transient response, position and rate accuracy, stiffness, and gimbal friction. A parameter sensitivity test and a discussion with recommendations close the main text. Illustrations show control moment gyros mounted in torque measuring fixtures on the load platform, the hardware the platform was built to exercise.
nasa-tm-19720023243-launch-vehicle-syste: Launch vehicle system requirements and restraints for the ERTS-A spacecraft is a NASA technical memorandum on launching an Earth resources satellite. The hosted sample is garbled optical character text, and it preserves no readable title page, author name, or date. Its abstract, kept with the record, says the report lists what the spacecraft required of the Delta launch vehicle. It also covers the shroud, the launch complex, and the range. Agencies involved in the launch could use those limits to coordinate their work.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-53-1-corinth:
First Corinthians, in the version of Douay-Rheims, an English rendering of the Latin Vulgate revised by Bishop Richard Challoner over 1749 to 1752. Its two parts first appeared at Rheims in 1582 and at Douay in 1609 and 1610. An introduction says Paul treats several matters of faith, morals, and church discipline in the letter.

Chapter one rebukes divisions about teachers. The world, Paul argues, was to be saved by preaching of the cross, not by human wisdom or fine speech. Paul writes as a called apostle, with Sosthenes, to a church in Corinth. Quarrels over leaders give the letter its start. From that local split, Paul moves to questions that still shape church teaching.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-54-2-corinth:
Second Corinthians, in Douay-Rheims English drawn from the Latin Vulgate, in the revision Bishop Richard Challoner finished across 1749 to 1752. Rheims in 1582 supplied the New Testament, Douay in 1609 and 1610 the Old Testament. An introduction says Paul recounts his sufferings and the graces God gave him. The letter was written in the same year as the first and sent by Titus from Macedonia.

Chapter one speaks of Paul's troubles in Asia. His failure to come was not levity, he insists, and his doctrine is constant and sincere. Paul writes with Timothy to the church at Corinth and all the saints nearby. Defence of his own ministry, unusual in a letter, fills much of what follows.
the-fourth-r:
George O. Smith wrote The Fourth R as a novel of a boy raised to a fierce pitch of learning, under a copyright of 1959. James Quincy Holden is five years old on the first page.

Jimmy's fifth birthday starts at seven with cocktails for the grown-ups, while he sips ginger ale. His gifts run to Kipling's Jungle Tales, a small planetarium, and a kit for building a Geiger counter with real samples to test. He picks the dinner menu and the music, then wins at bridge. Smith builds a tale of what a brilliant child, pushed by grown schemes, might do to the world that made him.
the-gutenberg-webster-s-unabridged-dicti:
Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary, in the version published in 1913 by the C. & G. Merriam Co. of Springfield, Mass., under the direction of Noah Porter, covers English words in alphabetical order. The portion here holds the letter R. It begins with a note on the letter itself, calling it a vocal consonant and a liquid, and tracing its form through Greek and Latin.

Word entries follow, each with pronunciation, origin, and sense. Early entries include Ra, the prefix Ra-, Raash for the electric catfish, Rab, and Rabat. The section also explains the phrase the three Rs for reading, writing, and arithmetic. Notes mark old or local uses and cite writers as support.
tom-swift-and-his-motor-cycle-or-fun-and:
Victor Appleton's first Tom Swift book opens on a country road, where two lads in a touring car urge red-haired Andy to shove the spark lever and make a record. Contents promise twenty-five chapters of fun and adventures on the road, starting with a narrow escape. Tom overhears something, suffers a smash-up, and gets his motor-cycle.

Later headings bring a vindictive tramp, men in an auto, a storm, a strange mansion, pursuit, and unexpected help. Mr. Swift despairs midway, and a man called Eradicate saws wood and gives a clue. Readers get the series launch, with speed and suspicion from the first page.
